passages.happening:
“Now Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, heard about all that God had done for Moses and His people Israel, and how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt” (verse 1).

Moses had sent his wife Zipporah back, and Jethro had taken her in, with her two sons (verses 2-3). “One son was named Gershom, for Moses had said, ‘I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.’ The other son was named Eliezer, for Moses had said, ‘The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh’” (verses 3-4).

Jethro comes with them to Moses in the desert, “where he was encamped at the mountain of God” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 17 one people, Amalek, came out to attack Israel. In chapter 18 another, Midian, comes out to welcome them. The contrast looks deliberate.

The Midianites lived on the edges of the desert, usually placed in northwest Arabia east of the Gulf of Aqaba, with groups ranging into the Sinai and the Negev. Genesis traces them to Midian, a son of Abraham by Keturah, so they too were distant relatives of Israel. Moses had fled to Midian as a young man, married Jethro's daughter, and was keeping Jethro's sheep when God called him at the bush (3:1). Now he is back at the same mountain, with the people he was sent to rescue.

The text does not say why Moses sent Zipporah back, or when. It simply tells us that Jethro had cared for her and the boys.

The names of the two sons tell Moses' life in brief. Gershom: a foreigner in a foreign land. Eliezer: the God of his father, his helper, who saved him from Pharaoh's sword.
passages.later:
God had promised Abraham, “I will bless those who bless you” (Genesis 12:3). The friendly Midianite and the hostile Amalekite stand side by side.

Judges remembers that Jethro's family went on with Israel: “Now the descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah” (Judges 1:16).
passages.asks: Jethro heard what God had done and came to see. Ask who around you has heard something of God's work in your life, and might want to hear the whole story. And ask how you could welcome them as Moses welcomed Jethro.

passages.t: ‘Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods’
passages.happening:
“So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent” (verse 7).

“Then Moses recounted to his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they had encountered along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them” (verse 8). “And Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel” (verse 9).

Jethro says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods, for He did this when they treated Israel with arrogance” (verse 11). He brings a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron and all the elders come “to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The welcome follows the customs of the time. Jethro sends word ahead. Moses goes out to meet him, bows, and kisses him. In Hebrew they ask after each other's shalom, their peace and well-being. A father-in-law was owed honor, and Moses gives it openly.

Then Moses tells the story. Not only the victories, but ‘all the hardships’ along the way too. Telling what God has done is how faith spreads.

And Jethro believes. ‘Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods.’ It sounds like the words of a newcomer coming to faith. A priest of another people hears the story and praises Israel's God.

The meal in verse 12 is more than hospitality. Eating together after a sacrifice, in God's presence, was a common way to seal friendship. The priest of Midian offers the sacrifices, and Aaron and the elders eat with him. A foreigner is welcomed at God's table.

Some scholars have proposed that Israel learned to worship the LORD from these Midianite in-laws. The text tells it the other way: Jethro learns from Moses what the LORD has done.
passages.later:
Rahab, another outsider, says something very like Jethro: “For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you” (Joshua 2:10), and “the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below” (Joshua 2:11).

The psalm says the same: “For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods” (Psalm 96:4). Matthew tells of Magi from the east who came to worship the child Jesus (Matthew 2:1-2). Jethro belongs in that line of outsiders who hear of God's acts and turn to him.
passages.asks: Moses told the whole story, hardships and all, and Jethro came to believe. Ask whether you tell others only the good parts of your walk with God, or the hard parts too. And ask who might come to know God through hearing your honest story.

passages.t: Judging alone, from morning to evening
passages.happening:
“The next day Moses took his seat to judge the people, and they stood around him from morning until evening” (verse 13).

Jethro asks, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone as judge, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?” (verse 14).

“‘Because the people come to me to inquire of God,’ Moses replied. ‘Whenever they have a dispute, it is brought to me to judge between one man and another, and I make known to them the statutes and laws of God’” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
In small societies, disputes were brought to a respected leader, who heard both sides in public and gave a ruling. Moses is doing that for a whole nation, all day, by himself.

He holds two roles at once. He decides cases, and he teaches God's laws. In Israel law came from God, not from a king.

The line of people stands there from morning until evening. They are tired, and so is he.
passages.later: Moses later remembers this: “I cannot carry the burden for you alone” (Deuteronomy 1:9). And again in Numbers: “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me” (Numbers 11:14).
passages.asks: Moses sat alone from morning until evening, and the people stood waiting. Ask whether you are carrying a load alone that God never meant you to carry by yourself. And ask who is standing in line, waiting, because you will not share the work.

passages.t: ‘What you are doing is not good’
passages.happening:
“But Moses’ father-in-law said to him, ‘What you are doing is not good. Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone’” (verses 17-18).

Jethro advises him: “You must be the people’s representative before God and bring their causes to Him. Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do” (verses 19-20).

“Furthermore, select capable men from among the people” (verse 21), men who are ‘God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain’. They will judge the smaller cases, and bring the major ones to Moses, “so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you” (verse 22). “If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns on the word ‘good’. Jethro rejoiced over all the ‘good’ God had done (verse 9). Now he says what Moses is doing is ‘not good’. It echoes God's words in Genesis 2:18: ‘It is not good for the man to be alone’.

Jethro sees what Moses cannot. The load is too heavy. He will wear himself out, and the people too.

Look at what Jethro asks for in the judges. Their qualities are moral before they are practical: men who fear God, men who can be trusted, men who hate dishonest gain. The groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens are like army divisions.

And notice how Jethro ends: ‘If ... God so directs you’. Good advice is still to be weighed before God.

A word of care. Leaders, pastors and caregivers often live in Moses' place, carrying too much, too long. Rest in Christ does not replace other help. If you are exhausted and it does not lift, or if weariness has turned into despair, please see a doctor or talk to a pastor or a crisis line. Weariness of body and mind can be illness, and getting care is not a lack of faith.
passages.later:
God later shares Moses' load with seventy elders: “They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself” (Numbers 11:17).

The apostles do something similar in Acts. They ask the church to choose seven men “confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom”, so that they can give themselves “to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:3-4).

The law forbids the dishonest gain Jethro warned against: “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8).
passages.asks: God used a foreign priest to give Moses wise counsel. Ask whether there is someone you have not been willing to listen to, because of who they are. And ask what part of your load you could share this week, so that you can endure.

passages.t: Judges appointed, and Jethro goes home
passages.happening:
“Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said” (verse 24).

“So Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And they judged the people at all times; they would bring the difficult cases to Moses, but any minor issue they would judge themselves” (verses 25-26).

“Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The great leader listens. Moses, who has spoken with God at the bush, takes advice from his father-in-law. Humility is part of leadership.

Hearing frames the whole chapter: Jethro ‘heard’ at the start (verse 1), and Moses ‘listened’ at the end (verse 24).

There is a puzzle about when this happened. Verse 5 has Israel already camped at the mountain of God, but their arrival at Sinai is told only in 19:1-2, and Deuteronomy remembers the judges being appointed around the time Israel left the mountain (Deuteronomy 1:9-18). Ancient Jewish interpreters already debated whether Jethro came before or after the law was given. Many think the chapter was placed here by theme, setting the friendly Midianite beside the hostile Amalekite. Others read it in order, with the courts set up during the long stay at the mountain.

Either way, the people who will hear God's law in the coming chapters are now organized into a community that can keep it.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy tells of the same appointment: “Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders” (Deuteronomy 1:13).

Hebrews speaks of one mediator who never needs relief: Christ “always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
passages.hard:
Is Moses' father-in-law named Jethro, Reuel or Hobab? He is Jethro here and in chapters 3 and 4, but Reuel in 2:18. Numbers 10:29 speaks of Hobab, son of Reuel, Moses' father-in-law, while Judges 4:11 seems to call Hobab himself Moses' father-in-law.

Several explanations are offered. Some suggest that Reuel was the head of the clan, perhaps Zipporah's grandfather, while Jethro was the father-in-law and Hobab his son. Others note that people in that world often had more than one name, and that Jethro may have been a second name or a title. Because the Hebrew words for father-in-law and son-in-law share the same letters, some read Hobab in Judges 4:11 as Moses' brother-in-law, as several English versions do. Many critical scholars see the different names as traces of different traditions woven together.

The difficulty is real, but small. Every account agrees that Moses married into a Midianite priestly family that treated him and Israel with kindness.
passages.asks: Moses listened to good advice and did it. Ask whether pride keeps you from taking counsel. And ask who has been a Jethro to you, and whether you have thanked them.
